title: Environmental economics

definition.text: The branch of economics that studies environmental problems and the economic effects of policies meant to deal with them.

facts.text: It weighs the costs and benefits of different policies on air pollution, water quality, toxic substances, solid waste and global warming.
Market failure, where markets do not put resources to their best use, is the idea at its centre.
Most environmental economists are trained as economists and use economic tools on problems where the market's 'invisible hand' cannot be relied on.
Putting an economic value on the environment is a major topic, because many natural resources carry no market price at all.
The name became popular in the 1960s, but links between economics and the environment go back to Condorcet, Adam Smith, Malthus and Ricardo.
Ronald Coase's economic solution to environmental problems is credited with settling it as a sub-field of economics.
It was once separate from natural resource economics, but the two are now hard to tell apart.
Its main professional bodies are the Association of Environmental and Resource Economists and the European Association for Environmental and Resource Economists.

notes: S:60b7b6319f6a says the field grew popular 'in the 19th century' in a section headed 20th Century; probably a slip for the 20th century.

definition.text: A cost or benefit that falls on a third party who had no part in the activity that caused it.

facts.text: Externalities are parts of production or consumption that carry no price.
Air pollution from cars is one: neither car makers nor drivers pay its cost to society.
Pollution of the environment is the textbook example of a negative externality.
Because the market price does not reflect the true cost or benefit to society, resources could be better allocated, so externalities are a kind of market failure.
Alfred Marshall first developed the idea in the 1890s, and Arthur Pigou brought it wider attention in the 1920s.
Governments often try to 'internalize' externalities so that prices include all the costs and benefits, most often by taxing whoever causes them.
Setting the right tax is hard because regulators rarely have full information about the externality.
The idea is now used beyond economics, in environmental science, public health and urban planning.

definition.text: A harmful side effect of producing or consuming something that lands on an unrelated third party and is not counted in the market price.

facts.text: It is also called an external cost or external diseconomy, and can arise in either production or consumption.
Formally, it is the gap between what an action costs the person taking it and what it costs society.
Air pollution from burning fossil fuels damages crops, materials, historic buildings and public health.
A neighbour's loud late-night music causing lost sleep is a consumption example.
Because they are Pareto inefficient, negative externalities are treated as more of a problem than positive ones.

definition.text: A beneficial side effect of an activity that helps an unrelated third party, without that party paying for it.

facts.text: It is also called an external benefit or external economy, and like a negative one can come from production or consumption.
A beekeeper's bees pollinate the crops around them as a side effect of honey production.
Planting trees makes nearby properties look nicer and cleans the surrounding area.
Even positive externalities are a market failure, because the good ends up produced below the best amount.
They invite free riding: a neighbour enjoying the bees for free has no reason to buy bees himself.

definition.text: A side effect in which one person's purchase of a status good lowers the value others get from similar goods they already own.

facts.text: It grows from the ideas of conspicuous consumption, buying to show off status, and positional goods, whose value depends on comparison with what others own.
When one member of a group buys a luxury car, others may feel they must upgrade too, wasting resources and widening inequality.
It can trigger a cascade of overconsumption as people spend to keep their relative standing.

definition.text: An externality that does not affect the marginal consumer, so it causes no market inefficiency.

facts.text: James Buchanan and Craig Stubblebine introduced the idea in 1962.
Because it acts only away from where the market clears, it does not misallocate resources and needs no policy action.

title: Causes of externalities

definition.text: The view that externalities come mainly from poorly defined property rights and from the costs of making trades.

facts.text: Land and money are easy to own, but air, water and wild animals cross borders freely, so people use them without paying the full cost.
A person who gets a flu shot cannot own a share of the herd immunity it creates, so may skip it.
Transaction costs, the costs of making a trade, block some worthwhile exchanges; without them people could bargain away every externality.

contested_note: The source page itself tags this section as one-sided, calling its property-rights account a narrow libertarian reading of Coase.

definition.text: A standard supply and demand graph with an extra curve added to show how an externality pushes the market away from the best quantity for society.

facts.text: For pollution, the private cost of making a good sits below its social cost by the amount of the external cost.
Buyers counting only private cost end up at a lower price and higher quantity than the efficient one.
Efficiency requires producing only while the marginal social benefit exceeds the marginal social cost.
In the steel example, people buy and use too much steel, and society would be better off if the extra units were never made.
With an external benefit such as vaccination, the private benefit falls short of the social benefit.
The gap is not fixed by competitive markets; some collective answer is needed, such as courts, bans or green taxes.

title: Ecological critique of externalities

definition.text: The argument from ecological and heterodox economists that treating environmental harm as an occasional 'externality' misreads how the economy works.

facts.text: Karl William Kapp called the term a misnomer, arguing that businesses shift costs onto others as a normal way of making profit.
Clive Spash argues that fixing the odd externality leaves the deeper, system-wide problem untouched.
Future generations, not yet born, cannot influence today's prices at all.
Heterodox economists instead argue for a theory of social costs that prevents harm through the precautionary principle.

contested_note: Ecological economists dispute the mainstream view that internalizing externalities can correct environmental harm.

title: Environmental versus ecological economics

definition.text: The contrast between environmental economics, which applies standard economics to the environment, and ecological economics, which treats the economy as a part of the ecosystem.

facts.text: Ecological economists stress 'strong' sustainability and reject the idea that human-made capital can stand in for natural capital.
Most environmental economists trained as economists, while most ecological economists trained as ecologists.
Ecological economics is described as more pluralistic and more focused on long-term sustainability and scale.
Environmental economics is seen as idealistic about the price system, ecological economics as more realistic about factors outside it.

contested_note: The two schools hold conflicting views traced to different philosophical foundations.

definition.text: Putting an economic value on the environment and natural resources, many of which have no market price.

facts.text: When natural assets go unpriced, they tend to be both overused and underinvested in.
Non-use values include existence value, option value and bequest value, such as wanting to leave a pristine environment to one's children.
Use values can be read from behaviour, such as the cost of recreational trips or house prices in hedonic methods.
Non-use values are usually estimated with surveys such as contingent valuation or choice modelling.
Contingent valuation asks people what they would pay for an environmental good, or accept for its loss.

definition.text: Government payments that reward companies more for exploiting natural resources than for protecting them.

facts.text: The damage these subsidies do to nature has been conservatively estimated at $4-$6 trillion U.S. dollars per year.
The largest support the fossil fuel, agriculture and water sectors.

definition.text: The value of nature that industries use up without paying for it, which would change their profits if it were priced.

facts.text: The world's largest industries burn about $7.3 trillion of free natural capital per year.
Those industries would hardly be profitable if they had to pay for this damage.
Cattle ranching and farming in South America ranks second, with a natural capital cost of 312.1 billion dollars against revenue of 16.6 billion.

definition.text: The social science that studies how goods and services are produced, shared out and used.

facts.text: It looks at how economic agents, such as households, firms, buyers and sellers, behave and interact, and how economies work.
Microeconomics studies individual agents and markets; macroeconomics studies whole economies, including growth, inflation and unemployment.
A widely accepted definition, from Lionel Robbins in 1932, calls it the study of human behaviour as a relationship between ends and scarce means that have alternative uses.
The word comes from the Ancient Greek oikonomia, the way to run a household; the field was earlier called political economy.
It separates positive economics, describing what is, from normative economics, arguing for what ought to be.
Adam Smith's The Wealth of Nations of 1776 is described as the birth of economics as a separate discipline; it named land, labour and capital as the factors of production.
Because controlled experiments are hard in economics, theories are mostly tested on observed data using econometrics.
Economic analysis is applied far beyond business, including to law, politics and the environment.

definition.text: A situation in which a free market's allocation of goods and services is not efficient, so economic value is lost.

facts.text: Mainstream economics lists several causes: monopoly power, externalities, public goods, missing or unequal information, unequal bargaining power, irrational behaviour, and unemployment or inflation.
Environmental economics deals mostly with externalities, also called 'public bads'.
Remedies include rules based on cost–benefit analysis or market tools that change incentives, such as emission fees or redefined property rights.
Governments often tax or restrict goods with negative externalities and subsidise goods with positive ones.
Most mainstream economists think government can sometimes improve the outcome, as with building codes or endangered species laws.
But government interventions can themselves misallocate resources, which is called government failure.
The term was first used by economists in 1958, though the idea is traced back to John Stuart Mill and Henry Sidgwick.

title: Ecological market failure

definition.text: A market failure in which economic activity exhausts vital non-renewable resources, damages fragile ecosystems or overloads nature's ability to absorb waste.

facts.text: Ecological economists argue that firms routinely shift social and ecological costs onto others, including future generations, so the market cannot exist without 'failing'.
Today's prices cannot reflect the wishes of people not yet born, so finite minerals are not shared fairly over time, an issue called intergenerational fairness.
Renewable resources with poorly defined property rights get overused, as in overfishing and overgrazing: the tragedy of the commons.
Climate change is presented as an overwhelming example, with the atmosphere as a global common with no clear property rights.
'Uneconomic growth' names the case where the ecological costs of more growth exceed its social benefits.
Herman Daly and Nicholas Georgescu-Roegen called for government limits on the overall level of economic activity.

contested_note: Ecological economists say most mainstream economists overlook these failures because Pareto efficiency ignores time.

definition.text: A market failure in which a firm or small group gains enough market power to block trades that would benefit both sides.

facts.text: It takes forms such as monopoly, monopsony and monopolistic competition.
Monopolies can last where barriers to entry keep other firms out.
Natural monopoly, sometimes caused by extreme economies of scale, is an extreme case.

definition.text: A market failure in which one side of a deal, such as an employer, can hold out longer than the other and so sets the terms.

facts.text: It has been used since the early 20th century to justify rules protecting workers, consumers and tenants.
Coase argued it only shifts income, but behavioural evidence shows unfair exchange lowers motivation to work, making it a real market failure.

definition.text: Unemployment, inflation and disequilibrium seen as market failures at the level of the whole economy.

facts.text: They can follow a financial crash, recession or depression, and show up as an economy producing below its capacity for a long time.
Business cycles of downswings and upswings are said to call for some government intervention.

title: Objections to market failure theory

definition.text: Arguments from several schools of thought that the idea of market failure is misleading, too narrow or does not justify government action.

facts.text: Public choice economists such as Milton Friedman argue that government failure may cost more than the market failure it tries to fix.
Some Austrian School economists deny that market failure exists, saying entrepreneurs seeking profit remove inefficiencies.
Marxian economists see inefficient outcomes as built into capitalism, not as rare exceptions.
High inequality is often called a market failure in everyday speech, but mainstream economics does not count it as one because it is not Pareto inefficient.
Zerbe and McCurdy note that, given transaction costs, market failure describes a situation that exists everywhere.

contested_note: Schools of economics disagree about whether market failure exists and whether it justifies government intervention.

definition.text: The basic fact that resources are limited, so only a limited amount of each good can be produced, while human wants have no such limit.

facts.text: Scarcity is central to economic theory and is said to be essential to a proper definition of economics itself.
There is never enough of something to satisfy every human want, even with advanced technology.
Scarcity forces sacrifice: getting more of one thing means giving something else up, a trade-off.
Market prices are one way to share out scarce resources.
Air matters more to us than gold yet is less scarce, because producing air costs nothing while gold must be found and processed.
A scarce good is one where more is wanted than is available at a price of zero.
Monopolies and stockpiling can create artificial scarcity, and panic buying can cause temporary scarcity.
Some argue that economic scarcity comes not only from limited resources but also from human activity and the way societies provide for themselves.

title: Absolute scarcity

definition.text: A condition in which basic human needs, such as food, exceed the quantities of useful goods available, linked to the ideas of Thomas Malthus.

facts.text: In his 1798 Essay on the Principle of Population, Malthus argued that more food raises well-being only for a while, because population then grows.
Malthusianism holds that population can grow exponentially while food supply grows only linearly.
Herman Daly describes absolute scarcity as the scarcity of resources in general, which rises as population and consumption approach the biosphere's carrying capacity.
Substituting one resource for another eases absolute scarcity but cannot remove it, according to Daly.

contested_note: Malthus's view on population and food has dominated debate on hunger for two centuries and remains disputed.

definition.text: A condition in which many different wants exceed the available means, which can be put to alternative uses, so people must choose.

facts.text: Mainstream economic theory stresses that it is relative scarcity that defines economics.
Lionel Robbins argued that when time and means are limited and ends can be ranked, behaviour necessarily takes the form of choice.
Every use of scarce means for one end gives up their use for another.
Paul Samuelson tied it to economic goods: without scarcity there would be no economic goods at all.

definition.text: The division of scarcity into demand-induced, supply-induced and structural kinds.

facts.text: Demand-induced scarcity comes when demand for a resource rises while supply stays the same.
Supply-induced scarcity, mostly caused by environmental degradation such as deforestation and drought, comes when supply is very low compared with demand.
Structural scarcity arises when part of a population lacks equal access to resources because of political conflict or location.
Supply-induced and structural scarcity cause the most conflict within a country.

definition.text: The presence in the air of substances that harm people, other living things or the environment.

facts.text: Pollutants may be gases such as ozone or nitrogen oxides, or small particles such as soot and dust, both outdoors and indoors.

Outdoor air pollution comes from burning fossil fuels for power and transport, wildfires, industry, waste, demolition and farming; indoor pollution often comes from burning wood or crop waste for cooking and heating.
It kills 7 to 8 million people each year, and particulate matter is its deadliest form.
The World Bank estimates its welfare and productivity losses cost the world economy over $8 trillion per year.
Many sources of local air pollution, especially fossil fuels, also release the greenhouse gases that cause global warming.
National laws such as Britain's 1956 Clean Air Act and the 1963 US Clean Air Act have often worked.
It is a standard example of an externality: neither makers nor users of cars pay its cost to society.

definition.text: The diseases and early deaths caused by breathing polluted air.

facts.text: It raises the risk of COPD, stroke, heart disease, lung cancer and pneumonia.
The 2024 Global Burden of Disease Study estimates it contributed to 8.1 million deaths in 2021, more than 1 in 8 deaths.
Outdoor fine particulate pollution caused the most of these deaths (4.7 million), followed by indoor particulate pollution (3.1 million) and ozone (0.5 million).
Burning fossil fuels is the largest source of air pollution deaths.
Global average life expectancy loss from air pollution in 2015 was 2.9 years, against 0.3 years from all direct violence.
Exposure in pregnancy makes stillbirth, miscarriage, birth defects and low birth weight more likely.

conflicts.text: The World Health Organization estimates 6.7 million deaths a year from air pollution.
conflicts.note: Different study (WHO) from the Global Burden of Disease figure of 8.1 million for 2021.

conflicts.text: A 2019 study estimated about 8.8 million deaths for 2015.

definition.text: The losses air pollution causes to economies through ill health, lost work, lower crop yields and other damage.

facts.text: It also harms tourism, biodiversity, forestry and water quality.
A World Bank study found PM2.5 pollution in 2019 cost the world economy over $8 trillion in health welfare costs; in India and China the loss was over 10% of GDP.
About 85% of that loss came from lives lost, priced using the value of a statistical life.
The OECD expects direct market costs from lost productivity, healthcare and crop losses to rise to 1% of GDP by 2060.
It even cuts solar power, by blocking sunlight and dirtying panels.

definition.text: The pattern in which poorer groups and some racial groups breathe more polluted air than others.

facts.text: Polluting industries and roads are more often placed in poorer communities, whose residents also more often work outdoors.
Low-income public housing residents who cannot easily move are heavily affected by nearby refineries and chemical plants.
Children are more exposed because they breathe faster and closer to the ground.

definition.text: The division of air pollutants into those released directly by a source and those that form in the air from other pollutants.

facts.text: Carbon monoxide from car exhausts and sulfur dioxide from factories are primary pollutants.
Secondary pollutants form when primary pollutants react with each other or the atmosphere; ground-level ozone is one.
Some pollutants are both emitted directly and formed from others.

definition.text: Ozone near the ground, formed mainly when nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds react in sunlight.

facts.text: It is the main gas in photochemical smog and peaks on hot summer afternoons.
It harms human health, materials, forests and crops, and reduces photosynthesis.
One study estimated that a 1% rise in ozone concentrations would cause a global economic loss of $10 billion each year.

title: History of air pollution control
article: Air pollution#Anti-smoke action and modern protections

definition.text: The story of how societies came to regulate air pollution, from early anti-smoke groups to international treaties.

facts.text: During the Industrial Revolution coal burning raised outdoor pollution sharply, yet city leaders saw black smoke as a sign of prosperity.
Early laws against pollution were weak because they were seen to clash with industrial interests.
The 1952 Great Smog of London killed some 12,000 people and led to the Clean Air Act 1956.
Acid rain spread across borders and needed international cooperation; ozone-damaging chemicals were later phased out by negotiation.

definition.text: Laws that set limits on pollutant concentrations in the air or on emissions from sources such as vehicles.

facts.text: 43% of countries lack a legal definition of air pollution, 34% lack outdoor air quality standards, and just 31% have laws on pollution from beyond their borders.
Few countries set limits as strict as the World Health Organization's recommendations, which are guidance rather than binding rules.
The Montreal Protocol, ratified worldwide, succeeded internationally, while climate action has been less successful.

definition.text: The losses in crop output and farm productivity caused by polluted air, especially ozone.

facts.text: A 1% rise in PM2.5 levels would cause about $5 billion in losses, especially in colder climates.
Pollution also lowers farm workers' productivity through its health effects.
Cleaner air during India's COVID-19 lockdown boosted greenness and photosynthesis, most strongly in crops.

definition.text: Economic waste caused by government action, when an intervention leaves resources worse allocated than some available alternative.

facts.text: It is the counterpart to market failure: government action meant to fix a market failure can itself fall short.
It happens when an intervention's costs outweigh its benefits, leaving society worse off than under another policy or none.
It is about inefficiency, not about who wins and loses: simply creating winners and losers is not a government failure.
It can come from any form of intervention: provision, taxes or subsidies, and regulation.
Common mechanisms include regulatory capture, unintended consequences, and inefficient outcomes that are easier politically than better ones.
The phrase became a term of art in the early 1960s; Ronald Coase used it in 1964, warning that all real social arrangements are more or less failures.
Public choice economists argue that government failure can be worse than the market failure it targets.
A small, well-organized interest group can pressure lawmakers into policies that do not benefit society as a whole.

definition.text: The main reasons government interventions go wrong, such as missing information, political pressure and short-term thinking.

facts.text: Governments find it hard to learn things such as production costs, so they may set quantities too high or too low.
Special interest groups can push politicians toward short-term gains.
Critics say politicians favour quick, visible fixes over lasting long-term solutions, called policy myopia.
Regulators who meet industry representatives often grow sympathetic and write rules that favour producers over society.

definition.text: The way taxes, subsidies and price controls can change prices artificially and disturb how markets share out scarce resources.

facts.text: Subsidies can waste scarce resources by shielding inefficient firms from market forces.
A price floor set above the market price, such as a minimum wage, can cause unemployment; a price ceiling set below it, such as rent control, causes shortages.
Taxes give people a reason to evade them.

definition.text: Sound that can harm the health of people and animals.

facts.text: Machines and transport are the main sources of outdoor noise worldwide.
Poor urban planning, such as industrial zones next to homes, can cause noise pollution in residential areas.
In the United States, noise is highest in low-income and racial minority neighbourhoods.
In animals, noise can raise the risk of death by disrupting how they detect predators or prey, and can interfere with breeding and navigation.
A neighbour's loud late-night music causing lost sleep is a textbook negative consumption externality.
Problems with urban noise are recorded as far back as ancient Rome.

definition.text: The harm that unwanted sound does to people's physical and mental health.

facts.text: It is linked to heart and circulation problems, high blood pressure, stress, tinnitus, hearing loss and disturbed sleep.
Noise-induced hearing loss can come from long exposure above 85 A-weighted decibels.
An estimated 113 million people in Europe face road traffic noise above 55 decibels, the level at which noise becomes harmful.
Occupational hearing loss is one of the most common work-related illnesses in the US and worldwide.

definition.text: The ways human-made noise disrupts animals that rely on sound to communicate, find mates, navigate and avoid predators.

facts.text: Noise from traffic, ships and aircraft can reach undisturbed habitats and affect species' survival.
Marine noise affects at least 55 marine species, and human-made ocean noise is doubling every decade.
Whales have changed migration routes and calls to avoid human-made noise.
Noise is now a prominent stressor on coral reefs, which communities depend on for fishing and tourism.

definition.text: Quantifying noise exposure as sound pressure levels in decibels, a logarithmic scale linked to how people hear.

facts.text: Road traffic and construction typically range from about 70 to over 100 dB, and repeated exposure above about 85 dB raises the risk of hearing damage.
Long-term community exposure is described with averaged measures such as the equivalent continuous sound level and the day–night average sound level.
Noise is measured with sound level meters, or with dosimeters worn by workers through a shift.

definition.text: The rules and methods governments and communities use to limit harmful noise exposure.

facts.text: Building codes and local ordinances may set maximum noise levels for homes, businesses and industry.
Noise barriers, speed limits, road surfaces and better planning reduce road noise.
Until the 1970s governments tended to treat noise as a nuisance rather than an environmental problem, and many disputes are still settled by negotiation between the noise maker and the hearer.
The US Noise Control Act of 1972 set a national policy against noise that endangers health and welfare.

definition.text: Pollution made of tiny particles suspended in air, water or space.

facts.text: Its three main forms are atmospheric particulate matter, marine debris and space debris.
Some particles are released directly and others form by chemical reactions in the air, from natural or human sources.
Sources include farming, cars, construction, forest fires and power plants.
There is no known safe level of exposure.
About 4.2 million premature deaths in 2016 were due to airborne particulate pollution, 91% of them in low and middle income countries.
US annual PM2.5 averages fell from 13.5 μg/m3 to 8.02 μg/m3 between 2000 and 2017 after tighter standards.

definition.text: The two main size classes of particulate matter: coarse particles of 10 micrometres and smaller, and fine particles of 2.5 micrometres and smaller.

facts.text: Fine particles can be breathed deep into the lungs and, with enough exposure, absorbed into the blood.
Worldwide, PM10 at 70 μg/m3 and PM2.5 at 35 μg/m3 have been shown to raise long-term mortality by 15%.
Older adults, children, pregnant women and people with weak immune systems face the greatest risk.

definition.text: A side effect that works only by changing market prices, not by changing the real resources available to others.

facts.text: City-dwellers buying second homes in the countryside can push up house prices for local young people.
It contrasts with technological or real externalities, such as factory pollution, which harm others directly.
In complete markets, buyers' losses from a price rise exactly match sellers' gains, so efficiency is kept; some economists say these are not really externalities.
When markets are incomplete or people face borrowing limits, they can matter for efficiency, which helps justify macroprudential regulation.

definition.text: A substance or form of energy put into the environment that has unwanted effects or makes a resource less useful.

facts.text: Pollutants may occur naturally, such as oil, or be made by people, such as manufactured materials and by-products.
They become pollution or a health concern once their concentration is high enough to do significant harm.
They can damage plant and animal growth, human health, resources people use, or property values.
Some break down naturally, but the breakdown products of others, such as DDT, are themselves pollutants.
Seen through planetary boundaries, people have released novel entities well beyond safe levels.
Because pollutants cross borders, international rules such as the 2004 Stockholm Convention on persistent organic pollutants are needed.

title: Stock and fund pollutants
article: Pollutant#Different types of pollutants in the environment

definition.text: The division of pollutants by how well the environment can absorb them: stock pollutants build up, fund pollutants are absorbed if emissions stay low enough.

facts.text: A pollutant only causes pollution once the environment's assimilative, or absorptive, capacity is exceeded.
Stock pollutants, such as PCBs, non-biodegradable plastics and heavy metals, accumulate over time, so damage grows and persists.
Stock pollutants burden future generations, with damage lasting long after the benefits are forgotten.
Fund pollutants, such as carbon dioxide absorbed by plants and oceans, cause harm only when emissions outpace absorption.
Fund pollutants are converted into less harmful substances or diluted, not destroyed.

definition.text: A way of grouping pollutants by where they do damage, horizontally (local or regional) and vertically (surface or atmosphere).

facts.text: Local pollutants harm areas near the source, while regional pollutants harm areas further away.
Surface pollutants build up near the ground, while global pollutants concentrate in the atmosphere.

definition.text: Concentration levels, such as the no-observed-adverse-effect level, used in risk assessment to decide how much of a chemical is safe.

facts.text: Industry keeps making new chemicals, and regulating them requires judging their danger to health and the environment.
Risk assessment is now seen as essential for making these decisions on a scientific basis.

definition.text: The release into the natural environment of contaminants that cause harm.

facts.text: It can be any substance, solid, liquid or gas, or energy such as heat, sound, light or radioactivity.
The word usually means contaminants from human sources such as manufacturing, mining, poor waste management, transport or farming.
It is classed as point source, from one concentrated site such as a factory, or nonpoint source, from widespread sources such as farm runoff.
In 2019 pollution killed about nine million people, about one in six deaths, roughly three-quarters of them from air pollution.
Polluting industries and waste sites are often placed near vulnerable and marginalized communities, a core reason for the environmental justice movement.
Economists treat pollution from manufacturing as a negative production externality, imposing health and clean-up costs on all of society.
Goods that pollute tend to be overproduced and underpriced because the harm is not priced into the market.
Many pollution sources went unregulated during industrialization until environmental regulation emerged in the later 20th century.

title: Socially optimal level of pollution

definition.text: The amount of pollution at which society's welfare is greatest, where the harm of one more unit equals the benefit of producing it.

facts.text: Society gets some indirect benefit from pollution, through polluting goods and lower prices; otherwise no one would pollute.
Policymakers must balance those benefits against pollution's costs to reach an efficient outcome.
Because the free market ignores pollution's cost to society, the true supply curve sits higher than the market one.
At the social optimum, output is lower and price higher than in the free market, so the free market outcome is a market failure.
The model is used to compare ways of internalizing the externality, such as tariffs, Pigouvian taxes like a carbon tax, and cap and trade.
It lies where the social marginal cost curve meets market demand.
Accepting some pollution can raise overall wellbeing, though every increase is still a cost that must be counted.
A corrective tax proportional to marginal damages yields the efficient level of pollution reduction.

notes: Phrase concept with no page of its own; Pollution#Socially optimal level is the closest section.

definition.text: What it costs a firm to cut the pollution it produces, called marginal abatement cost when measured per extra unit cut.

facts.text: Firms cut pollution by choice or because regulation forces them to.
In 2005 US pollution abatement capital and operating costs came to nearly $27 billion.

definition.text: The management of emissions and effluents released into air, water or soil.

facts.text: Without it, waste from farming, mining, manufacturing, transport and other activities would degrade the environment.
In the hierarchy of controls, preventing pollution and minimizing waste are preferred to controlling it afterwards.
Devices include wastewater biotreaters and constructed wetlands.

definition.text: How pollution grew from prehistoric fires to the industrial age and how societies began to respond.

facts.text: Greenland ice cores show pollution rising with Greek, Roman and Chinese metal production.
The Industrial Revolution created pollution as we know it today.
London's Great Stink on the Thames in 1858 led to the building of its sewer system.
Chicago and Cincinnati were the first American cities to pass clean air laws, in 1881.

title: Social cost

definition.text: The full cost of an activity to society: the private cost paid by those involved plus the external costs imposed on others who are not compensated.

facts.text: Private costs are the direct costs to the producer of making a good or service.
Driving's social costs include wear and tear, congestion and the pollution it causes others.
When social costs exceed private costs, relying on private markets alone gives an inefficient result.
The idea underlies the social cost of carbon, used to judge policies such as a carbon tax.
Pigou argued government should tax each unit by the marginal damage it causes; Coase argued affected parties could instead bargain.

contested_note: Whether government should intervene to correct social costs or leave it to bargaining is hotly debated.

title: Marginal social cost

definition.text: The total cost to society of producing one more unit of a good: marginal private cost plus marginal external cost.

facts.text: With a negative production externality such as steel pollution, marginal social cost is greater than marginal private cost.
Firms in a free market produce where marginal private cost meets marginal benefit, so they overproduce, creating a deadweight loss.
A tax equal to marginal damage raises private cost to match social cost.
With a positive externality, such as research and development, there is underproduction, which a Pigouvian subsidy can correct.
It is written MSC = MPC + MEC: marginal private cost plus marginal external cost.
Marginal private cost is the cost borne by the firm itself, and it is what businesses use when deciding how much to produce.
When marginal social cost exceeds private cost there is a negative externality; when it is lower, a positive one.
Production should rise only as long as the marginal social benefit exceeds the marginal social cost.

notes: Phrase concept with no page of its own.

definition.text: K. William Kapp's heterodox view that social costs are the share of production costs businesses shift onto society to raise profits.

facts.text: Kapp blames capitalist accounting laws that let producers leave these costs unpaid.
On this view capitalism is essentially a system of cost shifting, and legal cost shifting is a main source of profit.

definition.text: The difficulty of putting numbers on social costs, especially future, environmental and long-range harms.

facts.text: Environmental, social and political harms that span long periods are hard to predict and quantify, so hard to include in cost–benefit analysis.
Pricing carbon requires tracing a ton of greenhouse gas through temperature to crops, health, floods and ecosystems.
Costs from one firm in China can affect people's health in the United States, adding to the complexity.

definition.text: The way many small decisions, each insignificant on its own, can add up to a large outcome that nobody chose or wanted.

facts.text: Economist Alfred E. Kahn introduced the idea in a 1966 essay and described it as a common route to market failure.
Kahn's example was Ithaca's passenger railway, withdrawn because travellers' trip-by-trip choices did not cover its costs, though many would have paid to keep it.
Each choice of one option over another is also a vote to remove the other option, which may then disappear.

In 1982 ecologist William Odum applied it to the environment: almost 50 percent of the coastal marshlands of Connecticut and Massachusetts were lost between 1950 and 1970 through hundreds of small conversions.
Lake eutrophication, desertification and the plight of most endangered species are said to stem from series of small decisions.
A way to avoid it is to build and protect higher levels of decision-making, local to global, though these can push decisions back down.

definition.text: A peer-reviewed environmental economics journal, published twice a year, written to be readable by non-specialists.

facts.text: It is the official accessible journal of the Association of Environmental and Resource Economists.
It aims to bridge academic research journals and the general press on environmental economics and policy.
